title: Rural Single-Storey and Garden House Design 2027: Compact, Economical
desc: Designing single-storey (cấp 4) and garden houses in rural areas: whether a permit is needed, who may design, layout, heat protection, ventilation, cost tips.
summary: What to know when building a single-storey or garden house in the countryside: procedures, who designs, how to lay it out compactly and coolly, and how to save cost while keeping it durable and attractive.
body: p

The single-storey house (nhà cấp 4) and the one-floor garden house remain popular in rural areas because the cost is moderate, construction is quick and they suit family life. However, a small house does not mean building however you like: a sensible design from the start makes the house cooler, less prone to damage and avoids repair costs later.
h2
1. Does a rural single-storey house need a building permit?
p

Under Point g, Clause 2, Article 43 of the Construction Law 2025, a single-family house under 7 floors with a total floor area under 500 m² is exempt from a permit if it is not located in areas that already have planning, such as rural residential areas within an urban general plan, construction areas defined in the commune general plan, or areas that already have architectural management regulations.
p

Many hamlets already lie within the construction areas of the commune general plan, in which case a single-storey house still needs a permit. Ask the commune-level People's Committee before drawing the house; see also Which single-family houses are exempt from a building permit?.
h2
2. Who may design a single-storey house?
p

Under Point a, Clause 2, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP, the owner may organise the design personally when the house is at the same time: under 3 floors, without a basement, with a total floor area under 250 m² and under 12 m high. Most single-storey houses fall in this case. A large garden house with a total floor area of 250 m² or more must be designed by an organisation or individual with the relevant expertise and experience (Point b).
p

Even when self-designed, the house must still comply with standards and regulations and ensure safety for people and neighbouring works (Clause 1, Article 10). Hiring a qualified person to calculate the foundation and roof is usually much cheaper than the cost of dealing with cracks and settlement later.
h2
3. A compact layout suited to your way of life
ul
Simple massing (rectangle, L-shape): fewer corners, an easier roof, better waterproofing and savings in materials.
Living room and ancestral altar in the middle, bedrooms on either side; kitchen and bathrooms grouped on one side so pipes are short and easy to repair.
A wide front veranda: shades the doors from sun and rain and provides a place to sit and dry things.

Ancillary areas (farm tool store, animal pens, parking) separate from the living area, at the end of the wind direction. QCVN 01:2026 (in force from 1 January 2027) requires production and livestock works within a rural residential plot to have a waste collection and treatment system that ensures environmental hygiene (Section 4.5.2.5).
Leave yard and garden space so that rooms or a floor can be added later, if the foundation is designed in advance for that option.
h2
4. Cool, naturally lit, lower electricity bills
ul
The house orientation and main door should avoid the afternoon sun; use the region's prevailing wind and place doors opposite each other so the breeze crosses the room.
A pitched roof with a heat-insulating layer or ventilated ceiling; roof eaves that protect the walls from driving rain.
Trees and climbing frames on the harsh-sun side significantly reduce heat.
The regulation encourages rural housing suited to natural conditions and local architectural tradition and making use of local materials (note to Table 28, Section 4.5).
h2
5. Tips to save without hurting quality
ol
Finalise the drawings before starting work; changing them on paper is cheaper than changing them on site.
Do not cut back on the foundation, frame and waterproofing - the parts hardest to fix.
Choose common finishing materials that are easy to replace; invest selectively (doors, roof, bathroom).
Prepare an estimate and keep a contingency amount - see What costs a construction estimate includes.
h2
6. During construction
p

The owner must put up a site sign at the entrance showing the name, address and contact phone number; the owner organises construction and supervision and is responsible for the safety of the work, neighbouring works and the environment (Clause 3, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP).
p
Need advice on a single-storey or garden house within your budget? You can contact Quan Construction for support.
note

This article is for reference; every work needs to be surveyed and designed by a qualified person, suited to the actual land conditions and planning. QCVN 01:2026/BXD takes effect on 1 January 2027. For rules on building permits, ask the commune-level People's Committee where the land is located.
